body:
Why was the Indian National Congress established?

By the early 1880s, several Indian political associations had already demonstrated the value of organised discussion, petitions and public meetings. However, political activity was still divided among provincial organisations.

Indian leaders increasingly recognised that many grievances were common to different regions. Demands for greater Indian representation, fairer administration and economic relief could be presented more effectively through cooperation at the national level.

The Indian National Congress emerged from this process of growing political awareness and efforts to establish an all-India organisation.

The first Congress session

The first session of the Indian National Congress was held at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College in Bombay from 28 to 30 December 1885.

It brought together 72 delegates from different parts of British India. Participants included lawyers, journalists, social reformers and other educated public figures.

Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee, commonly written as W. C. Bonnerjee, presided over the first session.

Allan Octavian Hume, a retired British civil servant, played a major organisational role in establishing the Congress and bringing Indian political leaders together. He also served as its first General Secretary.

First Congress session

  • Year: 1885.
  • City: Bombay, now Mumbai.
  • Venue: Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College.
  • Delegates: 72.
  • First President: W. C. Bonnerjee.
  • Important organiser: A. O. Hume.

The role of A. O. Hume and Indian political leaders

Hume's organisational role was important, but the Congress should not be understood as an organisation created without Indian political initiative.

Before 1885, Indian leaders such as Dadabhai Naoroji, Surendranath Banerjee, Ananda Mohan Bose, Pherozeshah Mehta and others had already been developing political associations and national cooperation.

Hume helped coordinate these existing political efforts. The Congress consequently brought together Indian nationalist initiative and the organisational assistance provided by Hume.

The first session gave the developing nationalist movement a regular platform through which delegates could discuss grievances and present common demands.

Early objectives of the Congress

The Congress did not initially adopt complete independence as its immediate objective. Its early programme concentrated on national political cooperation and reforms within the existing constitutional framework.

Its principal objectives included:

  • National unity: Encouraging cooperation among politically active Indians from different provinces, religions and communities.
  • Political education: Developing public awareness of government policies, rights and administrative grievances.
  • Common demands: Identifying important issues affecting Indians and presenting coordinated representations to the government.
  • Representative government: Seeking greater Indian participation in legislative councils and public administration.

These objectives were important because political activity had previously been organised mainly within regional associations. The Congress created a regular opportunity to discuss Indian affairs from a broader national perspective.

Important early Congress sessions

1886: Calcutta

The second Congress session took place in Calcutta in December 1886 under the presidency of Dadabhai Naoroji.

The number of delegates increased to 434, according to the Congress's own historical record. The session also decided to establish Provincial Congress Committees, helping the organisation develop a more regular structure across India.

1887: Madras

The third session was held in Madras in December 1887 under the presidency of Badruddin Tyabji.

Tyabji became the first Muslim President of the Indian National Congress. His presidency reflected the Congress's stated aim of representing Indians across religious communities.

1888: Allahabad

The fourth session took place in Allahabad in December 1888 under the presidency of George Yule.

George Yule became the first British President of the Indian National Congress.

1890: Calcutta

The sixth session was held in Calcutta in December 1890 under the presidency of Pherozeshah Mehta, an important Moderate leader associated with Bombay politics.

What changed after 1885?

The Congress helped convert the activities of regional political associations into a more regular national political programme.

Its annual sessions enabled leaders from different parts of India to exchange views, adopt resolutions and communicate common demands.

However, the early Congress remained dominated by educated urban groups. Its claim to represent the interests of the Indian people was broader than the actual social composition of its membership.

Thus, the foundation of the Congress was an important step towards organised nationalism, but it did not immediately create the mass national movement that developed in later decades.

Prelims focus

  • First Congress session: Bombay, 1885, W. C. Bonnerjee.
  • First session venue: Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College.
  • First session attendance: 72 delegates.
  • Second session: Calcutta, 1886, Dadabhai Naoroji.
  • Third session: Madras, 1887, Badruddin Tyabji.
  • Fourth session: Allahabad, 1888, George Yule.
  • Trap: A. O. Hume helped establish the Congress but was not its first President.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 9, printed pp. 110–111; Indian National Congress, INC Sessions, sessions of 1885–1890, consulted 20 November 2026; Indian National Congress, Brief History of Congress, entries for 28 December 1885 and 27 December 1886, consulted 20 November 2026; Indian National Congress, Synopsis of Plenary Sessions from 1885 to 2018, entry for the first session and General Secretary, consulted 20 November 2026.]

body:
What was the Moderate phase?

The period from approximately 1885 to 1905 is commonly known as the Moderate phase of the Indian National Congress.

During these years, the Congress was largely led by nationalists who believed that political reforms could be secured through constitutional methods, public discussion, petitions and appeals to British principles of justice.

The term Moderate describes their political objectives and methods. It does not mean that these leaders approved of every British policy or avoided criticism of colonial rule.

Constitutional methods

Constitutional methods are forms of political activity that seek change through legally recognised institutions and procedures. The early nationalists used petitions, resolutions, public meetings, legislative discussions and representations to government authorities rather than attempting to overthrow colonial rule through armed action.

Important Moderate leaders

Dadabhai Naoroji

Dadabhai Naoroji was among the most influential early nationalist leaders. A Parsi public figure associated with Bombay and London, he played an important role in explaining Indian political and economic grievances to British audiences.

He established the East India Association in London in 1866, became Congress President in 1886 and developed the influential economic criticism known as the Drain of Wealth Theory.

In 1892, he became the first Indian elected to the British House of Commons, representing Central Finsbury as a Liberal Party member.

His career demonstrated how early nationalists attempted to influence both Indian public opinion and British political institutions.

Pherozeshah Mehta

Pherozeshah Mehta was an important political leader associated with Bombay. He helped establish the Bombay Presidency Association in 1885 and was an influential advocate of representative institutions and constitutional reform.

He presided over the Congress session at Calcutta in 1890.

Gopal Krishna Gokhale

Gopal Krishna Gokhale was an influential Moderate leader associated with Poona. He supported constitutional reform, greater Indian participation in administration, public education and the use of reasoned argument in political affairs.

His political approach placed considerable importance on developing public institutions and preparing Indians for greater responsibility in government.

Surendranath Banerjee

Surendranath Banerjee helped establish the Indian Association in 1876 with Ananda Mohan Bose.

Through public speaking, political campaigns and organisational activity, he encouraged cooperation among educated Indians from different regions.

He was associated with the Indian National Conference and later became an important Congress leader.

Other important Moderates

  • W. C. Bonnerjee: First President of the Indian National Congress.
  • Badruddin Tyabji: Important Bombay leader and first Muslim Congress President.
  • Romesh Chandra Dutt: Nationalist economic thinker who examined the effects of colonial economic policies.
  • Dinshaw Edulji Wacha: Bombay-based nationalist associated with public finance and Congress activity.
  • G. Subramania Iyer: Important figure in southern Indian political and journalistic activity.
  • Mahadev Govind Ranade: Influential reformer and political thinker associated with the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha.

How did the Moderates conduct political activity?

Petitions and memorials

A petition is a formal request submitted to an authority. A memorial, in this historical political context, was a written representation explaining a grievance or seeking a reform.

The Moderates submitted such documents to colonial officials and British authorities. They attempted to demonstrate that particular policies were unjust, economically harmful or inconsistent with accepted principles of good government.

Congress resolutions

At its annual sessions, the Congress discussed important questions and adopted resolutions.

A resolution expressed the organisation's formal position on an issue, such as the need to expand legislative councils or reduce military expenditure.

Passing a resolution did not itself change the law. It established a common political demand that Congress representatives could communicate to the government and the public.

Public meetings and newspapers

Moderate leaders organised public meetings, delivered speeches, wrote newspaper articles and circulated arguments concerning colonial government.

These activities helped develop political awareness and explain the reasons behind nationalist demands.

Newspapers were especially important because they enabled political arguments to reach readers who could not attend particular meetings.

Appeals to British political institutions

The Moderates also attempted to influence political opinion in Britain, where important decisions about Indian government were made.

They sought support among sympathetic British politicians and communicated Indian grievances through public meetings, publications and parliamentary contacts.

Dadabhai Naoroji's activities in Britain were a prominent example of this approach.

Why did the Moderates believe these methods would work?

Many early nationalist leaders had studied British constitutional institutions and liberal political ideas. They believed that British people and politicians could be persuaded to recognise the injustice of discriminatory administration and economic exploitation.

They therefore placed considerable faith in the effectiveness of reasoned argument, accurate information and sustained public pressure.

Their approach was also influenced by practical circumstances. The nationalist movement was still developing its organisation and public support, while the colonial government possessed extensive political and administrative powers.

The Moderates generally hoped to achieve reforms gradually rather than immediately attempting to end British rule through direct confrontation.

Was Moderate politics merely petitioning?

Petitions were central to their methods, but Moderate political activity was broader than submitting requests.

The Moderates criticised British policies, organised meetings, influenced newspapers, investigated economic grievances and attempted to mobilise public opinion.

These activities contributed to the development of political awareness even when the government rejected particular demands.

Moderate politics and its limitations

The Moderates primarily sought reforms through constitutional methods. Their critics later argued that petitions and appeals depended too heavily on British willingness to cooperate. The disagreement concerned the effectiveness of political methods as well as the pace and extent of reform.

The connection with Gujarat

Several important early nationalist leaders belonged to Gujarati Parsi communities and were closely associated with political activity in Bombay. Dadabhai Naoroji, Pherozeshah Mehta and Dinshaw Wacha are important examples.

The Bombay Presidency included much of present-day Gujarat. Consequently, political activity centred in Bombay also formed part of the wider environment in which nationalism developed in Gujarat.

The Gujarat Sabha in Ahmedabad provides another example of early constitutional political organisation in the region.

Prelims focus

  • The Moderate phase is commonly dated 1885–1905.
  • Dadabhai Naoroji: East India Association, economic drain critique and British Parliament.
  • Pherozeshah Mehta: Bombay Presidency Association and Congress President in 1890.
  • Surendranath Banerjee: Indian Association, 1876.
  • Gopal Krishna Gokhale: constitutional and administrative reform.
  • Moderate methods: petitions, resolutions, public meetings, newspapers and representations.
  • Trap: Moderate nationalism involved criticism and public political activity; it was not unconditional support for British rule.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 9, A Nation in the Making, printed pp. 111–112; Press Information Bureau, Dadabhai Naoroji: The Man Who Brought Statistics into Politics, 27 June 2017, consulted 20 November 2026; Press Information Bureau, Sir Surendranath Banerjea, biographical discussion of political organisation, consulted 20 November 2026; Indian National Congress, INC Sessions, founding-period presidential records, consulted 20 November 2026; Drishti IAS, To What Extent Did the Role of the Moderates Prepare a Base for the Wider Freedom Movement?, 17 January 2022.]
